intro.headline: Every website you ship started on one computer.
intro.lede: A scroll-through story of how the web got from a cube on a desk to code running in hundreds of cities. Turn your sound on.

lines.e1l01: March 1989. A physics lab under the Swiss–French border.
lines.e1l02: Thousands of scientists. Their documents sit on machines that can't talk.
lines.e1l03: Tim Berners-Lee writes a memo: “Information Management: A Proposal”.
lines.e1l04: His boss, Mike Sendall, scribbles on it: “Vague but exciting…”
lines.e1l05: Christmas 1990. A <g_server>server</g_server> and a <g_browser>browser</g_browser> called <g_wwwapp>WorldWideWeb</g_wwwapp> are running.
lines.e1l06: Three ideas: HTML to write pages, HTTP to fetch them, URLs to find them.
lines.e1l07: The whole web lives on one <g_nextcube>NeXTcube</g_nextcube>, on Tim's desk.
lines.e1l08: Taped to the front: a warning. Go on, peel it back.
lines.e1l09: Few can run that browser. Nicola Pellow writes a line-mode browser for any terminal.
lines.e1l10: Try it. Type a number. Press Enter.
lines.e1l11: 6 August 1991. Tim posts it to the alt.hypertext <g_newsgroup>newsgroup</g_newsgroup>. Anyone can join.
lines.e1l12: Cambridge, 1991. The <g_trojan>Trojan Room</g_trojan> coffee pot is a long walk away. So they point a camera at it.
lines.e1l13: Not video. A tiny grey photo, about three times a minute. Empty? Stay put.
lines.e1l14: 30 April 1993. CERN makes the web free for all. No fees. No patents.
lines.e1l15: 1993: the pot goes on the web. Reload to see the latest photo.
lines.e2l01: 1993, NCSA. Marc Andreessen and Eric Bina release Mosaic. Pictures appear inline.
lines.e2l02: Everybody wants a <g_homepage>homepage</g_homepage>. First, get online.
lines.e2l03: That screech is two modems shaking hands. At 28.8k, 100 KB takes 28 seconds.
lines.e2l04: Pages are files. To answer you, the server runs a program: CGI.
lines.e2l05: Every click: a new process, a full reload. Nobody minds. It's magic.
lines.e2l06: 1995. Rasmus Lerdorf writes PHP to see who reads his résumé.
lines.e2l07: Spring 1995. Netscape hires Brendan Eich to build a browser language. Fast.
lines.e2l08: He writes it in about ten days. Mocha, then LiveScript, then JavaScript.
lines.e2l09: <g_netscape>Netscape</g_netscape> versus <g_ie>Internet Explorer</g_ie>. The <g_browserwars>browser wars</g_browserwars> begin. Each invents its own tags.
lines.e2l10: 1996. Håkon Wium Lie's CSS arrives. We keep using '<'table> and '<'font>.
lines.e2l11: Where does a site live? A beige tower in the office closet.
lines.e2l12: A <g_geocities>GeoCities</g_geocities> page, a <g_webring>webring</g_webring>, a <g_hitcounter>hit counter</g_hitcounter>. Sign the <g_guestbook>guestbook</g_guestbook>.
lines.e2l13: <g_y2k>Y2K</g_y2k> passes quietly. Then the <g_dotcom>dot-com bubble</g_dotcom> pops. Many companies don't survive.
lines.e3l01: 1 April 2004. Gmail launches with 1 GB free. Rivals offer a few MB. A joke?
lines.e3l02: Mail opens without reloading, thanks to XMLHttpRequest. Microsoft added it in 1999.
lines.e3l03: 2005. Jesse James Garrett names the trick Ajax. It powers Web 2.0.
lines.e3l04: <g_gmaps>Google Maps</g_gmaps> lets you drag the planet around. Go on, grab it.
lines.e3l05: Browsers disagree on everything. 2006: John Resig's jQuery hides the mess.
lines.e3l06: Everyone has a <g_blog>blog</g_blog>. Vote on a story: it re-sorts, no reload.
lines.e3l07: Ruby on Rails and Django make a database-backed site a weekend project.
lines.e3l08: Sites live in rented racks: a <g_lb>load balancer</g_lb>, some <g_server>servers</g_server>, one big <g_mysql>MySQL</g_mysql>.
lines.e3l09: 2006. AWS rents servers by the hour. Stop buying hardware.
lines.e3l10: 2007. The <g_iphone>iPhone</g_iphone> ships a real <g_browser>browser</g_browser>. No <g_flash>Flash</g_flash>. Screens get small.
lines.e4l01: 2009. Ryan Dahl puts V8 on the server: Node.js. JavaScript runs everywhere.
lines.e4l02: 2016. An 11-line npm package, left-pad, is unpublished. Builds break worldwide.
lines.e4l04: <g_jsconf>JSConf US</g_jsconf>, 2013. <g_react>React</g_react> debuts and lots of developers hate it. <g_jsx>HTML inside JavaScript</g_jsx>?
lines.e4l05: The <g_server>server</g_server> sends a nearly empty page. The <g_browser>browser</g_browser> builds the rest.
lines.e4l06: Fast once running. Slow to start. Hard for search engines to read.
lines.e4l07: 2014. Evan You releases Vue, a lighter take on the idea.
lines.e4l08: Code sits on a CDN. The API sits on Heroku. Deploy with git push.
lines.e4l09: Design <g_flat>goes flat</g_flat> and <g_responsive>responsive</g_responsive>. One layout, phone to desktop.
lines.e4l10: Everything is a feed, and <g_infinite>the feed never ends</g_infinite>. Try it.
lines.e5l01: 2016. Guillermo Rauch's team releases Next.js. React renders on the server again.
lines.e5l02: The pendulum swings back between server and browser.
lines.e5l03: Static sites return too, <g_ssg>pre-built</g_ssg> on a <g_cdn>CDN</g_cdn>. Call it the <g_jamstack>JAMstack</g_jamstack>.
lines.e5l04: Rich Harris asks: what if the framework compiled itself away? Svelte.
lines.e5l05: 28 February 2017. An engineer debugging <g_s3>S3</g_s3> in <g_useast>us-east-1</g_useast> mistypes one command.
lines.e5l06: Four hours of broken sites. Even the status page breaks. Its icons live in <g_s3>S3</g_s3>.
lines.e5l07: Now the server sends the shell first and streams the rest as it's ready.
lines.e5l08: Some components run only on the <g_server>server</g_server>, talking straight to the database.
lines.e5l09: Where does it live? Everywhere. <g_edgefn>Edge functions</g_edgefn> run milliseconds from you…
lines.e5l10: …but the data still lives in one place. <g_latency>Light only travels so fast</g_latency>.
lines.e5l11: Today's stack: <g_typescript>TypeScript</g_typescript>, <g_vite>Vite</g_vite>, and often one <g_monorepo>monorepo</g_monorepo> for everything.
lines.e5l12: Shipping is one command. Go on, push to <g_production>production</g_production>.
lines.e6l01: The next reader of your website might not be a person.
lines.e6l02: AI <g_agent>agents</g_agent> can now use a <g_browser>browser</g_browser>. Give one an errand. It asks before paying.
lines.e6l03: 29 September 2025. US shoppers buy from Etsy sellers without leaving a chat.
lines.e6l04: Search becomes answers. With an AI summary, people click a result 8% of the time, not 15%.
lines.e6l05: Sites push back. <g_cloudflare>Cloudflare</g_cloudflare> blocks <g_aicrawler>AI crawlers</g_aicrawler> by default, or charges them.
lines.e6l06: Next: <g_webmcp>WebMCP</g_webmcp> hands <g_agent>agents</g_agent> real tools, not buttons to guess at. Flip the views.
lines.e6l07: <g_agent>Agents</g_agent> get ID cards and wallets: <g_x402>x402</g_x402>, <g_ap2>AP2</g_ap2>, <g_acp>ACP</g_acp>. None has won yet.
lines.e6l08: Speculation from here. Every site gets two audiences: people and their agents.
lines.e6l09: The pendulum gets a third pole. Not where it renders, but who's reading.
lines.e6l10: Wild guesses: <g_a2a>agents haggling with agents</g_a2a>, throwaway apps, a <g_robots>robots.txt</g_robots> war. Rate them.
lines.e6l11: Six eras. Six desks. The same three ideas from 1990. <g_agent>Agents</g_agent> speak them too.

fin.headline: From one cube in Geneva to everywhere.
fin.body: The web keeps swinging between the server and the browser. Where it swings next is up to the people who build it, which now includes you.

term.p1:
WHAT'S OUT THERE?

About 50 web servers exist by January 1993.

SLAC, Stanford[5]: first server outside Europe, December 1991.
CERN phone book[6]
term.p2:
HELP

Type the number of a link and press RETURN.
B = back, H = home, Q = quit.
term.p3:
PEOPLE

Tim Berners-Lee: proposal, first server and browser
Robert Cailliau: co-wrote the 1990 proposal
Nicola Pellow: this line-mode browser
Jean-François Groff: libwww
term.p4:
HISTORY

1989 Mar  First proposal
1990 Nov  Formal proposal, with Robert Cailliau
1990 Dec  First server and browser running
1991 Aug  Announced on alt.hypertext
1993 Apr  Released into the public domain
term.p5:
SLAC

Paul Kunz saw the web at CERN, went home to California, and put SLAC's physics paper database on it.
term.p6:
CERN PHONE BOOK

One of the web's first popular uses: looking up a colleague's phone number.

aria.d1: Diagram: the first web server was a single NeXTcube on Tim Berners-Lee's desk at CERN, reached over the CERN Ethernet by terminals running the line-mode browser and over slow leased lines by a few dozen labs and universities, including SLAC in California.
aria.d2: Diagram: a home PC dials through a modem and phone line to an ISP modem pool, across the internet backbone, to one beige tower in an office closet running Apache, Perl or PHP, and MySQL.
aria.d3: Diagram: a laptop on DSL reaches a colocation data center where a load balancer spreads requests over three LAMP servers backed by memcached and MySQL. From 2006 the same setup could be rented as EC2 virtual servers and S3 storage.
aria.d4: Diagram: a phone first downloads a JavaScript bundle from a CDN, then the app running in the phone's browser calls a JSON API on platform-as-a-service dynos, which reads from a managed Postgres database. The client devices are highlighted because the app now runs there.
aria.d5: Diagram: a world map with edge locations in many cities. A phone in Jakarta reaches a nearby Singapore edge function in about 10 milliseconds, which fetches data from a database in the US East region about 220 milliseconds away and streams HTML back. Below, a pipeline: git push, build, deploy everywhere, preview URL.
aria.d6: Diagram: a person sends an intent to their AI agent. The agent passes a signed request through a bot gate to a shop's WebMCP tools, reads a news site's llms.txt, and sends a payment token to a bank.

d5.far: ~220 ms round trip to the data

d2.note: a 100 KB page at 28.8 kbit/s ≈ 30 s
